nameStory: The Redhead gets its straightforward name from the male's striking copper-red head that looks like burnished metal in the sunlight. This distinctive feature makes it one of the most aptly named ducks in North America, though it's also been called the red-headed duck and red-headed pochard by those who appreciate being extra descriptive!
description: The Redhead is a medium-sized diving duck that's built for life on deeper waters. Males sport that famous copper-colored head along with a black chest, gray back, and pale blue bill, while females are a more subdued brownish color overall. These sturdy ducks measure 16-22 inches long with a wingspan of nearly three feet, weighing about as much as a large chicken (around 2-2.5 pounds).

idTips.label: Male's Copper Head
idTips.description: The male's head gleams like a new penny in sunlight - a rich, reddish-copper color that's unmistakable when you see it. The color appears almost metallic and contrasts sharply with the black chest.

idTips.label: Rounded Head Shape
idTips.description: The head has a distinctly rounded, almost ball-like profile rather than the sloped or angular look of similar ducks. This gentle curve is visible from the side and gives the bird a softer appearance.

idTips.label: Pale Blue Bill
idTips.description: The bill appears powder blue or blue-gray, like faded denim, and feels smooth if you could touch it. It's shorter and stubbier than you might expect for a diving duck.

idTips.label: Yellow Eyes (Male)
idTips.description: Males have bright yellow eyes that stand out like golden coins against their copper heads. These eyes have an almost glowing quality in good light.

idTips.label: Diving Behavior
idTips.description: Watch them disappear completely underwater for 10-30 seconds at a time, popping back up like corks. Unlike dabbling ducks, they don't just tip forward - they vanish entirely beneath the surface.

idTips.label: Female Coloring
idTips.description: Females are warm brown overall with a slightly lighter, more golden-brown head. They have the same rounded head shape and blue bill as males but lack the dramatic color contrast.

habitat: Look for Redheads on larger, deeper lakes and ponds throughout New England, especially those with plenty of open water for diving. They prefer waters with submerged vegetation like pondweed and wild celery, and you'll often spot them in coastal bays and estuaries during migration. They need deeper water than puddle ducks since they dive completely under to feed.

seasonality.spring: Males arrive in peak breeding plumage with their most vibrant copper heads and bright yellow eyes. This is when the color contrast between males and females is most dramatic, making identification easiest.
seasonality.summer: Most Redheads breed further north and west, so summer sightings in New England are uncommon. Any birds present are likely non-breeding individuals or early migrants.
seasonality.fall: Peak migration time brings the most Redheads through New England waters. Males may be in duller transitional plumage, but the distinctive head shape and bill color remain reliable identification features.
seasonality.winter: Small numbers winter in ice-free coastal areas and larger inland lakes. Males retain much of their distinctive coloring through winter, though it may appear slightly less vibrant than during breeding season.

funFact: Redhead females are notorious for being "nest parasites" - they sneak their eggs into other ducks' nests and let the unsuspecting foster parents raise their babies, kind of like the duck version of a cuckoo bird!
confusionNotes: The Canvasback is the most likely mix-up, but remember: Redheads have a rounded head like a baseball, while Canvasbacks have a sloped, wedge-shaped head like a ski jump. If the head looks like it could roll down a hill, it's probably a Canvasback!
compareHints: Among its Aythya relatives in New England, the Redhead's rounded head shape sets it apart from the wedge-headed Canvasback, while its copper (not dark) head distinguishes it from Ring-necked Ducks and scaups. The male's yellow eyes are also unique - Canvasbacks have red eyes, and most other Aythya ducks have dark eyes.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among its Aythya relatives, Ring-necked Duck is the small, vegetarian cousin with the white bill ring.
Compared to Ring-necked Ducks, Greater Scaup lack the white ring around the bill and have much more white on their sides and back.
Among New England's diving ducks in the same genus, Lesser Scaup are most similar to Greater Scaup but have rounder heads and shorter wing stripes.
Among its diving duck relatives, canvasbacks are much larger than ring-necked ducks and scaup, with that unique sloping head profile no other Aythya duck shares.
Among its Aythya relatives, Tufted Duck is most similar to Ring-necked Duck but has the distinctive drooping head tuft and golden (not yellow) eyes.
Among its Aythya relatives in New England, male Common Pochards most resemble Redheads but have deeper red heads and darker eyes.
